children.translated_text: 'Attached to the coils of a serpent,
Thus, of those [examples] pervaded by <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning)
and of others that should be inferred,
When, by something engaged in a different matter,
The sun, even as it rises,
to demonstrate that the fruit of prosperity
the host of darkness meets defeat —
this instantly indicates the miserable end
of those opposed to a king.
and pale, together with my limbs,
and [adorned] with the moon [as I with pallor].
together with the swooning of travelers,
The spring days, beautiful with the songs of cuckoos,
increase together with the delight of people —
some description of its form is made:
By the arm of yours that deals blows of weapons
<s>Āśīḥ</s> (benediction) is the expression of a wish
for a desired thing, as follows:
which is beyond the reach of speech and mind.'
A variant of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) is just that,
and a sub-type of <s>utprekṣā</s> as well;
The relation of principal and subordinate
the beauty of your face, O innocent one;
for those equipped with stalk-staffs [i.e., an army],
Darkness smears, as it were, the limbs;
the sky rains down, as it were, collyrium;
like the service of wicked men,
<s>bhāva</s> is the intention of the poet
that remains in the poem until its completion.
of all elements of the subject-matter,
the description of settings without [unnecessary] action,
the manifestation of even profound subject-matter
by the force of the sequence of expression —
thus they know it as <s>bhāvika</s> (having imaginative realization).
And what in other treatises — [those on] dramatic junctures,
sub-divisions, modes of conduct, characteristics, and the like —
has been described, this is treated by us
This path has been laid open, summarizing in measured fashion
the infinite expanse of the figures of speech;
the distinctions that revolve beyond the scope of words —
practice alone is sufficient to unfold them.

children.text: // ity ācārya-daṇḍinaḥ kṛtau kāvyādarśe 'rthālaṃkāravibhāgo nāma dvitīyaḥ paricchedaḥ //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second chapter, named 'The Division of Figures of Meaning,' in the <s>Kāvyādarśa</s> composed by the teacher <s>Daṇḍin</s>.
